items.title: Dominic James "Nick" La Rocca Interview, 1958-05-26
items.q: I think I played in the last record, one of his records.

ctx.x: Well, this is a Memphis bank and it's on Charles Handy.

Handy. That's correct. That's where they kept the account. The original name was from Memphis, Tennessee. It was called Pace and Handy, the original friend. Now, this Negro recorded. After Ralph Pell. I think this man runs a southern music company today, if I'm not mistaken. After our big success on Broadway and rising, that was January the 15th, which we opened there. And the sensation we created was something that they had never heard of in 50 years on Broadway. Anyway, the Columbia company, trying to get…
Now, Mr. LaRocco, I want to tell you that we made some tapes Saturday night of Raymond Burke, who used to work with you. You remember?

items.title: Dominic James "Nick" La Rocca Interview, 1958-05-21
items.q: So they went to Memphis, Tennessee, and they selected W.C. Handy, who was to become the father of jazz and creator of the blues, and who couldn't either play blues or jazz.

I guess you've noticed the stop time in both records. This record was played probably 10 years or 12 years before Armstrong's record was played. I'll let you know how far the colored man has come.

Playing a tiger rag. This is Dixonland Jubilee by Kit Ory. This is only about a year old. Between this and the one that I'll play that was played almost 42 years ago, 41 years ago, you'll see the difference. That's what these white men call good music. Some of these tribes should go back in Africa and live over there and find out about the Negro place over there. This man is coming Louis Armstrong. That's Armstrong.
